words.definition: Learning facts by repeating them until they are memorised, rather than by understanding them.
words.example: Critics argue that an overemphasis on rote learning produces students who can recall facts but struggle to apply them to unfamiliar problems.

words.definition: The ability to analyse information objectively, question assumptions and reach a reasoned judgement.
words.example: Schools should place greater emphasis on critical thinking so that young people can evaluate the claims they encounter online.

words.definition: Practical instruction that prepares people for a particular trade or job, such as plumbing, nursing or engineering.
words.example: Expanding access to vocational training could reduce youth unemployment by giving school leavers the skills that employers actually need.

words.definition: Education at university or college level, which follows secondary school.
words.example: In many developed nations, the proportion of young people entering tertiary education has risen dramatically over the past three decades.

words.definition: The money that students pay to a university or college for their teaching.
words.example: Abolishing tuition fees would make higher education accessible to talented students from low-income families.

words.definition: The level of success someone reaches, especially in education, usually measured by grades or qualifications.
words.example: Research consistently shows a strong correlation between parental involvement and pupils' academic attainment.

words.definition: Having a broad range of skills, knowledge and experiences rather than being good at only one thing.
words.example: Sport, music and drama help schools to produce well-rounded individuals rather than mere exam-passers.

words.definition: Describing activities, such as clubs or sports teams, that students do in addition to their normal lessons.
words.example: When budgets are squeezed, extracurricular activities are often the first to be cut, even though they build confidence and teamwork.

words.definition: The ability to understand and work with numbers in everyday situations.
words.example: Employers frequently complain that a significant minority of school leavers lack basic literacy and numeracy.

words.definition: The process of continuing to gain knowledge and skills throughout your life, not only at school or university.
words.example: As automation reshapes the labour market, lifelong learning is no longer a luxury but an economic necessity.

words.definition: The methods and practice of teaching, and the theory behind them.
words.example: Advances in educational technology have prompted a fundamental rethink of traditional pedagogy.

words.definition: Describing a class or group that contains students with different levels of ability.
words.example: Proponents of mixed-ability classes argue that weaker pupils benefit from learning alongside more able peers.

words.definition: The percentage of students who leave a school or course before completing it.
words.example: The dropout rate among first-year undergraduates tends to rise sharply when financial support is withdrawn.

words.definition: To give someone the skills, knowledge or qualities they need to do something.
words.example: The primary purpose of schooling should be to equip young people with the skills to thrive in adult life.
collocations: be well equipped to cope with

words.definition: A system in which people succeed because of their ability and effort rather than their wealth or social background.
words.example: Unless access to good schools is equalised, the claim that education creates a meritocracy rings hollow.

words.definition: Involving practical experience of doing something rather than just studying it in theory.
words.example: Hands-on experience gained through internships is often valued more highly by employers than a degree alone.

words.definition: A system of exams in which all students answer the same questions and are marked in the same way, so that results can be compared.
words.example: An excessive reliance on standardised testing encourages teachers to teach to the test at the expense of genuine understanding.
